title: Motown and Soul
objective: After this level you can describe Motown and soul music.
summary: Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in 1959 with an $800 loan and ran it like an assembly line. Soul returned to gospel and blues; Aretha Franklin's Respect (1967) became an anthem.

cards.headline: The Motor City built cars. Then a former assembly-line worker built hits.
cards.body: In January 1959, Berry Gordy Jr. founded a record company in Detroit with an $800 loan from his family. A two-story house on West Grand Boulevard became its studio and headquarters, nicknamed Hitsville. Motown grew into one of the most successful Black-owned businesses in American history. How do you build hits the way Detroit built cars?

cards.headline: A factory for songs
cards.body: Gordy said a brief stint on an auto-plant assembly line taught him how to make a quality product. So Motown ran like a line: in-house songwriting teams such as Holland-Dozier-Holland, a house band called the Funk Brothers, and strict quality control. Britannica credits Motown with the highest hit ratio for released singles of any record company in history. Its records were even mixed to sound good on car radios. Detroit, naturally.

cards.headline: Soul: back to church and the blues
cards.body: Alongside Motown's polish ran soul music, an African American style that grew from the 1950s into the 1970s. Britannica calls it a return to the roots of gospel and blues: church-style call and response, intense singing, long melodic runs. Ray Charles helped start it by turning gospel songs into secular ones. Remember Sister Rosetta Tharpe, who played gospel on electric guitar in Level 73? Same church, different road.

cards.headline: "Respect": one song, two movements
cards.body: Otis Redding wrote and first recorded "Respect." Aretha Franklin, raised singing in the Baptist church, reworked it: she spelled out R-E-S-P-E-C-T and added "sock it to me." It topped the Billboard Hot 100 on June 3, 1967, and became an anthem for civil rights and women's equality, even though Franklin said she had recorded it as a song about a man and a woman.

learned: 1959: Berry Gordy founds Motown in Detroit with an $800 loan

Soul: a return to gospel and blues roots

questions.prompt: Where and how did Berry Gordy Jr. start Motown in 1959?

options.label: In Memphis, with money from Sam Phillips
options.rationale: Phillips ran Sun Records in Memphis; Motown was Gordy's.

options.label: In Liverpool, with a deal from EMI
options.rationale: Motown was American through and through.

options.label: In Detroit, with an $800 loan from his family
In New York, funded by NBC
options.rationale: It began with a family loan, not a network.

questions.explanation: Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in January 1959 with an $800 family loan.

questions.prompt: What idea did Berry Gordy bring from the auto plant to Motown?

options.label: Recording songs inside a real car factory
options.rationale: The studio was a house called Hitsville.

options.label: Specialized teams and strict quality control, like an assembly line
Making every song exactly the same length
options.rationale: The lesson was about quality, not length.

options.label: Letting each singer write and play everything alone
options.rationale: Motown did the opposite, with house writers and a house band.

questions.explanation: Gordy said the assembly line taught him about quality; Motown had house songwriters, a house band and strict quality control.

questions.prompt: From Level 61: soul's church-style call and response has the same shape as the spirituals. What is that shape?

options.label: Two melodies moving note against note
options.rationale: That's organum; call and response trades lines.

options.label: A leader sings a line and a group answers
Every singer improvising a different tune
options.rationale: One voice leads and the group replies.

options.label: A soloist singing with no one replying
options.rationale: In call and response, the group answers the leader.

questions.explanation: Spirituals were built on call-and-response, a leader's line answered by the chorus, and soul returned to that church-style exchange.
